note: HAND-WRITTEN plain-language descriptions, for a reader who has never encountered a substance and does not know what it is. PsychonautWiki cannot supply these: its `summary` field is a scraped warning box that is frequently junk ("Summary sheet: MDMA MDMA"), and its `effects` field returns only the substance's own name. Both were checked against the live API on 2026-08-10 before writing these by hand.
rules: Say what it IS and what people take it FOR. Someone who does not know cannot assess a warning about it.
No dosing, no route advice, no how-to. Dose ranges already live in their own section with their own caveats.
Neither advertise nor frighten. 'Euphoric' oversells; 'deadly poison' is the fear-based framing EVIDENCE.md rejects. Describe.
Name the ordinary medical use where there is one - most people meet oxycodone, ketamine and diazepam in a hospital first.
Plain words. Roughly an 8th-grade reading level, no pharmacology unless it changes what someone would do.

descriptions.alcohol: The drug in beer, wine and spirits. It is a depressant, meaning it slows down the brain and body — which is why it makes people relaxed and unsteady, and why it becomes dangerous alongside other depressants like opioids or benzodiazepines. It is legal and ordinary, and that is exactly why it is easy to forget it belongs on this list at all.
descriptions.cannabis: The dried flower of the cannabis plant, smoked, vaped, or eaten in food. Effects vary widely between people and between strains — commonly relaxation, altered senses, hunger, and for some people anxiety or a racing heart instead. Eaten, it takes far longer to come on than smoked, which is the single most common way people take more than they meant to.
descriptions.mdma: A stimulant with emotional effects, usually sold as ecstasy or molly, in pills or powder. People take it for warmth, closeness and energy, mostly in social and music settings. It raises body temperature and heart rate, and what is sold under these names frequently is not MDMA.
descriptions.lsd: A psychedelic, usually sold on small squares of blotter paper. It changes perception, thought and mood for a long time — commonly eight to twelve hours, which is far longer than most people expect the first time. It is not associated with fatal overdose, but a difficult experience can be genuinely distressing and is influenced heavily by mood, company and surroundings.
descriptions.psilocybin-mushrooms: Mushrooms containing psilocybin, sometimes called magic mushrooms or shrooms, usually eaten dried or brewed as tea. They produce visual changes, shifts in thought and mood, and often strong emotion, for around four to six hours. The main physical risk is misidentifying a wild mushroom, not the psilocybin itself.
descriptions.ketamine: An anesthetic used in hospitals and in veterinary medicine, also used recreationally as a powder. It produces detachment from the body and surroundings, and at higher amounts a state where someone cannot move or interact — which is dangerous around vomiting, water, or being left alone. Regular heavy use is strongly linked to serious bladder damage.
descriptions.cocaine: A stimulant made from the coca plant, sold as a white powder. It produces alertness, confidence and energy for a short time — often under an hour — which is why people redose. It strains the heart, and the combination with alcohol produces a third substance in the body that is harder on the heart than either alone.
descriptions.crack-cocaine: Cocaine processed into a smokable rock. Same drug as powder cocaine, but smoking delivers it faster and the effect ends sooner, which makes redosing more frequent and dependence more likely to develop.
descriptions.heroin: An opioid made from morphine, sold as a powder or sticky tar. It produces pain relief, warmth and heavy sedation. What is sold as heroin in much of the US now contains fentanyl, or is fentanyl — which is why the strength of a supply can change without warning between one batch and the next.
descriptions.fentanyl: A synthetic opioid used in hospitals for severe pain, and now the dominant opioid in the illicit supply. It is active in far smaller amounts than heroin, so it is difficult to mix evenly — meaning two parts of the same batch can differ in strength. It is frequently present in drugs not sold as opioids at all.
descriptions.methamphetamine: A long-acting stimulant, sold as crystals or powder. It produces alertness, energy and wakefulness for many hours — much longer than cocaine. Long or heavy use is associated with sleep loss, weight loss, dental problems, and paranoia or psychosis that can persist after stopping.
descriptions.amphetamine: A stimulant, prescribed as Adderall for ADHD and also used non-medically. It increases focus, energy and wakefulness and reduces appetite. Prescribed and illicit versions are the same drug; what differs is that a prescription has a known strength.
descriptions.methylphenidate: A stimulant prescribed as Ritalin or Concerta, mainly for ADHD. It sharpens focus and increases energy, with a shorter action than amphetamine.
descriptions.alprazolam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Xanax for anxiety and panic. It is a depressant: it calms, sedates, and impairs memory of the period it is taken. Combined with opioids or alcohol it is one of the most common contributors to fatal overdose, and pressed pills sold as Xanax often contain something else entirely.
descriptions.diazepam: A benzodiazepine, prescribed as Valium for anxiety, muscle spasm and alcohol withdrawal. Longer-acting than most others in its family. Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause seizures, so it is one of the few drugs where quitting abruptly is more dangerous than tapering.
descriptions.oxycodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as OxyContin or Percocet. It relieves pain and produces sedation and euphoria. Pills sold as oxycodone outside a pharmacy — particularly ones marked M30 — are very often pressed fentanyl instead.
descriptions.codeine: A weaker opioid found in some prescription cough syrups and pain tablets. The body converts it to morphine, and how much it converts varies a lot between people, so the same amount affects two people differently.
descriptions.buprenorphine: An opioid used to treat opioid dependence and pain, prescribed as Suboxone or Subutex. It occupies opioid receptors without producing the same effect, which reduces withdrawal and cravings. Because it holds on so tightly, taking it too soon after another opioid can trigger sudden withdrawal.
descriptions.tramadol: A prescription painkiller that acts as a weak opioid and also affects serotonin. That second action makes it interact badly with antidepressants and raises seizure risk, so it does not behave like other opioids of similar strength.
descriptions.kratom: The leaf of a Southeast Asian tree, taken as powder, capsules or tea. In smaller amounts it acts more like a stimulant, in larger amounts more like a mild opioid. Some people use it for pain or to manage opioid withdrawal. Regular use can produce dependence and its own withdrawal.
descriptions.ghb: A depressant, sold as a salty liquid, used recreationally and sometimes for sleep. Its defining hazard is that the gap between the amount that produces an effect and the amount that causes unconsciousness is unusually narrow. Combined with alcohol that margin narrows further.
descriptions.dmt: A short, extremely intense psychedelic, usually smoked or vaped. Effects arrive within seconds and are typically over within fifteen to thirty minutes. It is also the active component of ayahuasca, where combining it with a MAOI makes it last hours instead — and introduces serious interactions with many medications.
descriptions.mescaline: A psychedelic found in peyote, San Pedro and related cacti, traditionally used in Indigenous ceremony. It produces visual and emotional changes lasting roughly ten to twelve hours. Peyote is slow-growing and threatened, and its ceremonial use is legally protected for members of the Native American Church.
descriptions.2c-b: A synthetic psychedelic with stimulant qualities, sold as pills or powder. Shorter than LSD, typically four to eight hours. It sits in a family of closely related chemicals with quite different strengths, and mistaking one for another is the usual way people get into trouble with it.
descriptions.nitrous: Nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, used in dentistry and to charge whipped cream canisters. Inhaled, it produces about a minute of dizziness and distortion. The specific risks are suffocation if it is breathed without oxygen, and nerve damage from repeated heavy use, which depletes vitamin B12.
descriptions.pregabalin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain, seizures and anxiety, sold as Lyrica. It is a depressant and adds to the sedating effect of opioids and alcohol, which is why it appears in overdose reports more often than its reputation suggests.
descriptions.gabapentin: A prescription medicine for nerve pain and seizures, sold as Neurontin. Like pregabalin it is sedating and stacks with opioids and alcohol. It is often assumed to be harmless because it is common and freely prescribed.
descriptions.methadone: A long-acting opioid, used both to treat opioid dependence and for pain. It lasts much longer than heroin or fentanyl — often over a day — which is what makes it useful for stopping withdrawal, and also what makes it dangerous: it builds up in the body over the first days of taking it.
descriptions.morphine: The original opioid painkiller, made from the opium poppy and still used in hospitals for severe pain. Most other opioids are measured against it.
descriptions.hydrocodone: An opioid painkiller, prescribed as Vicodin or Norco, usually combined with paracetamol. That combination matters: taking extra tablets for more opioid effect also raises the paracetamol dose, which damages the liver.
descriptions.hydromorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Dilaudid, used in hospitals for severe pain. Considerably stronger than morphine for the same amount.
descriptions.oxymorphone: A strong opioid painkiller, prescribed as Opana. Stronger than oxycodone for the same amount.
descriptions.tapentadol: A prescription painkiller that acts as an opioid and also affects noradrenaline. Like tramadol, that second action means it interacts with antidepressants in ways other opioids do not.
descriptions.pethidine: An older opioid painkiller, also called meperidine or Demerol, once common in childbirth and surgery. Now used less because a breakdown product builds up with repeated doses and can cause seizures.
descriptions.dihydrocodeine: An opioid painkiller similar in strength to codeine, found in some prescription tablets and cough preparations.
descriptions.o-desmethyltramadol: What the body turns tramadol into, and the part that actually relieves pain. It is also sold on its own, sometimes in products claiming to be herbal — which is a problem, because the strength is unknown and it carries tramadol’s seizure risk.
descriptions.dextropropoxyphene: An opioid painkiller withdrawn from the US and much of Europe because it caused heart rhythm problems and deaths at doses not far above normal ones.
descriptions.acetylfentanyl: A fentanyl analogue, meaning a chemical cousin of fentanyl. It was never made as a medicine and turns up in the illicit opioid supply. Like fentanyl it is active in very small amounts, so it is hard to mix evenly.
descriptions.sufentanil: A hospital opioid, used in surgery and epidurals. Far stronger than fentanyl for the same amount, and not something with a safe margin outside a clinical setting.
descriptions.u-47700: A synthetic opioid, sometimes sold as pink or U4. It was made for research, never approved as a medicine, and appears in the illicit supply as a powder or pressed into counterfeit pills.
descriptions.dextromethorphan: The cough suppressant in many over-the-counter cold medicines, often labeled DXM. In larger amounts it acts as a dissociative, producing detachment and altered perception. The main practical danger is cold medicines that also contain paracetamol or antihistamines, which become toxic long before the DXM effect ends.
descriptions.pcp: A dissociative anaesthetic, also called angel dust, abandoned for medical use because of the confusion and agitation it caused on waking. It produces detachment from the body and surroundings, and unpredictable effects on mood and behavior.
descriptions.mephedrone: A stimulant, also called 4-MMC or meow meow, sold as a powder or in capsules. It produces energy and sociability for a short time, which tends to lead to redosing.
descriptions.3-mmc: A stimulant closely related to mephedrone, sold after mephedrone was banned in many countries. Similar effects, similarly short-lived.
descriptions.a-pvp: A long-acting stimulant, sometimes called flakka, related to the cathinones. Effects can persist for many hours and it is associated with agitation, sleeplessness, and confusion at higher amounts.
descriptions.methylone: A stimulant with mild emotional effects, chemically related to MDMA but noticeably weaker in that respect. It has been sold as, or mixed into, things labeled MDMA.
descriptions.mda: A psychedelic stimulant closely related to MDMA, sometimes called sally. Longer-lasting than MDMA with more visual effect and less of the emotional warmth.
descriptions.mdea: A drug closely related to MDMA, sometimes called eve, with milder emotional effects.
descriptions.gbl: A liquid solvent that the body converts into GHB, with the same effects and the same narrow gap between the amount that produces an effect and the amount that causes unconsciousness. It acts faster than GHB, which makes that gap harder to judge.
descriptions.baclofen: A prescription muscle relaxant for spasticity, sometimes used for alcohol dependence. It is a depressant and adds to the effect of opioids and alcohol. Stopping it abruptly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal.
descriptions.mdai: A drug related to MDMA that produces emotional warmth with little stimulation. Sometimes sold as a legal substitute for MDMA.
descriptions.5-apb: A stimulant with psychedelic qualities, sold as a substitute for MDMA and often lasting considerably longer than expected.
descriptions.6-apb: A stimulant with psychedelic qualities, sometimes called benzo fury, sold as an MDMA substitute. It comes on slowly, which is the usual way people take more than they meant to, and lasts a long time.
